title: What happens if a service crashes during an update using asynchronous communication, and how do you handle it (ack+retry, idempotency, DLQ, transactional outbox, circuit breaker, saga)?
shortTitle: What happens if a service crashes during an update using asynchronous communication

s1_definition.profdef: In asynchronous communication a consumer may crash at any point: after receiving a message but before processing, mid-processing, or after processing but before acknowledging. The broker's delivery guarantee determines recovery. With manual acknowledgment and at-least-once delivery, an unacknowledged message is redelivered after the crash, so the work is retried. To make redelivery safe you need idempotency so reprocessing does not double-apply, a dead-letter queue for poison messages that always fail, a transactional outbox so a producer never loses an event, a circuit breaker to stop hammering a failing dependency, and a Saga to coordinate and compensate multi-step workflows.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, imagine a back-office clerk takes a transfer slip from the inbox tray and starts working, but faints halfway. If the rule is "only move the slip to the done tray after the work is fully finished", then when the clerk recovers, the slip is still in the inbox, so it gets picked up again and redone. To make sure Rajesh is not charged twice when the slip is redone, each slip has a unique stamp the clerk checks first. Slips that keep causing fainting are moved to a special problem tray for a supervisor.
s1_definition.oneliner: A crash means the unacknowledged message is redelivered, so you survive it with manual ack plus retry, idempotent processing, a dead-letter queue for poison messages, a transactional outbox so events are never lost, and a Saga with compensation for multi-step work.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In asynchronous communication a consumer may crash at any point: after receiving a message but before processing, mid-processing, or after processing but before acknowledging. The broker's delivery guarantee determines recovery. With manual acknowledgment and at-least-once delivery, an unacknowledged message is redelivered after the crash, so the work is retried. To make redelivery safe you need idempotency so reprocessing does not double-apply, a dead-letter queue for poison messages that always fail, a transactional outbox so a producer never loses an event, a circuit breaker to stop hammering a failing dependency, and a Saga to coordinate and compensate multi-step workflows.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, imagine a back-office clerk takes a transfer slip from the inbox tray and starts working, but faints halfway. If the rule is "only move the slip to the done tray after the work is fully finished", then when the clerk recovers, the slip is still in the inbox, so it gets picked up again and redone. To make sure Rajesh is not charged twice when the slip is redone, each slip has a unique stamp the clerk checks first. Slips that keep causing fainting are moved to a special problem tray for a supervisor.

**One line to remember:** A crash means the unacknowledged message is redelivered, so you survive it with manual ack plus retry, idempotent processing, a dead-letter queue for poison messages, a transactional outbox so events are never lost, and a Saga with compensation for multi-step work.

sections.s2_technical:
First understand exactly where a crash can happen and what the broker does. With at-least-once delivery and manual acknowledgment, the consumer receives a message, processes it, and only then sends an acknowledgment. If it crashes before acknowledging, the broker sees the message was never acknowledged and redelivers it to another consumer or to the same one after restart. This guarantees the work is not lost, but it means the same message can be delivered more than once, which is the central challenge.

Acknowledge and retry is the foundation. You configure manual acknowledgment so the message is only acknowledged after the business work has durably committed, never on receipt. In Spring Kafka this is `ack-mode: MANUAL` and calling `acknowledgment.acknowledge()` after the database commit. On a transient failure you let the message be redelivered, often with a backoff so you do not hammer a struggling dependency. For example a `DefaultErrorHandler` with an exponential backoff retries a few times before giving up.

Idempotency makes redelivery safe. Because the same message may arrive twice, processing must produce the same result whether it runs once or five times. You achieve this with an inbox table of processed message ids, a unique constraint on a natural key, or state-based checks. For example before crediting Priya you check whether this message id is already in the processed table; if it is, you skip and acknowledge. This is the single most important defense, because without it at-least-once delivery corrupts balances.

A dead-letter queue handles poison messages. Some messages will never succeed, perhaps because of malformed data or a permanent downstream rejection. If you retry forever you block the partition and starve good messages. After a bounded number of retries you route the message to a dead-letter queue, where it waits for human inspection while normal processing continues. For example the error handler is configured with a `DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer` that publishes to `transfer.events.DLT` after three failed attempts.

The transactional outbox protects the producer side. The danger there is the dual-write problem: if you update the database and then publish an event as two separate steps, a crash between them loses the event. The outbox pattern writes the event into an outbox table in the same database transaction as the business change, so they commit atomically, and a separate relay reads the outbox and publishes to the broker, retrying until it succeeds. A crash can never leave a committed business change without its event.

A circuit breaker protects against cascading failure. If the downstream the consumer calls is down, retrying every message immediately wastes resources and worsens the outage. A circuit breaker trips open after a threshold of failures, fails fast for a cool-down period, then half-opens to test recovery. For example a Resilience4j circuit breaker around the fraud-check call stops the worker from flooding a dead service.

Finally, a Saga coordinates multi-step workflows that span services. If a crash happens partway through a sequence of local transactions across services, you cannot use a distributed database rollback, so a Saga runs compensating transactions to undo the steps that already committed. For example if payment succeeded but shipment scheduling failed after a crash-and-retry, the Saga issues a refund to compensate. A senior nuance is that these mechanisms compose: the outbox guarantees the event is published, at-least-once plus manual ack guarantees it is delivered and retried, idempotency guarantees redelivery is safe, the DLQ contains poison, the circuit breaker protects the dependency, and the Saga keeps the overall workflow consistent.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A consumer at National Bank of India credited Priya's account from a `MoneyTransferred` message, then crashed before acknowledging. On restart the broker redelivered the message and the consumer credited Priya a second time, double-counting the money. This is exactly why we need idempotency with a processed-message inbox so the second delivery is detected and skipped.

Problem 2 — One malformed message with a null account id failed on every retry and blocked the partition, starving all later transfers. This is exactly why we need a dead-letter queue, so after a few attempts the poison message is parked and good messages flow again.

Problem 3 — A producer updated the ledger and then crashed before publishing the event, so a downstream service never learned about the transfer. This is exactly why we need a transactional outbox so the event is written atomically with the ledger change and relayed reliably.

Our mini-project builds a resilient transfer consumer. The code defines a `TransferEvent`, an `InboxStore` of processed message ids for idempotency, a `TransferConsumer` that processes with manual acknowledge-after-commit, retries transient failures, and routes poison messages to a dead-letter queue, a `DeadLetterQueue`, and a demo that delivers the same event twice to prove idempotency and delivers a poison event to prove the dead-letter path.

# Run

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: valid event MSG-001 crediting CUR3001 by 50000, redelivered once; poison event MSG-999 with a null target.

Step 1: MSG-001 arrives. The consumer calls `inbox.claim("MSG-001")`, which atomically records the id and returns true because it is the first time. It credits Priya from 250000 to 300000 and only then acknowledges. The acknowledgment happens after the credit, which is the key ordering.

Step 2: A crash is simulated and the broker redelivers MSG-001. The consumer calls `inbox.claim("MSG-001")` again, which now returns false because the id is already recorded. It logs a duplicate and skips the credit, then acknowledges. Priya's balance stays at 300000, so redelivery was safe.

Step 3: MSG-999 arrives with a null target. Processing throws a poison exception immediately because the data is permanently invalid. The consumer does not retry a poison message; it routes it straight to the dead-letter queue.

Step 4: The dead-letter queue now holds MSG-999 with the reason, where a human or an automated reprocessor can inspect it, while normal processing continues unblocked.

Step 5: The final state shows Priya credited exactly once at 300000 and one message parked in the dead-letter queue, demonstrating that at-least-once delivery with idempotency and a DLQ survives both crashes and poison data.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Event MSG-001 {to:CUR3001, amount:50000}
    │
    ▼
  TransferConsumer.onMessage
    │ inbox.claim("MSG-001") → TRUE (first time)
    │ balances.credit(CUR3001, 50000) → 250,000 → 300,000
    │ ACK (only AFTER commit)
    │
  ── CRASH + redelivery of MSG-001 ──
    │
    ▼
  TransferConsumer.onMessage
    │ inbox.claim("MSG-001") → FALSE (already processed)
    │ skip credit (idempotent no-op)
    │ ACK
    ▼
  CUR3001 = Rs.300,000 not double-counted

  Event MSG-999 {to:null}
    │
    ▼
  process → PoisonException("null target")
    │ no retry (permanent)
    ▼
  DeadLetterQueue.publish(MSG-999, "null target account")
    → partition unblocked, good messages continue

  ── Producer side (not shown in demo but required) ──
  business update + outbox row  → SAME DB transaction (COMMIT)
  outbox relay → Kafka (retry until published)  ← no event ever lost
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The first thing I establish is exactly what happens at a crash. In asynchronous messaging with at-least-once delivery and manual acknowledgment, a consumer only acknowledges a message after the work has durably committed, so if it crashes before acknowledging, the broker sees the message was never acknowledged and redelivers it. That means no work is lost, but the same message can be delivered more than once, and that duplicate delivery is the central problem I have to design around.

My layered defense starts with acknowledge-and-retry. I configure manual acknowledgment so a message is acknowledged only after the business change commits, never on receipt, and on a transient failure I let it be redelivered with a backoff so I do not hammer a struggling dependency. The single most important layer on top of that is idempotency, because at-least-once delivery will replay messages and I must get the same result whether a message runs once or five times. I implement that with an inbox table of processed message ids, a unique constraint on a natural key, or a state-based check, so a redelivered message is detected and skipped instead of double-applying a credit.

Then I add the other mechanisms for the cases retry alone cannot solve. A dead-letter queue catches poison messages that will never succeed, so after a bounded number of retries they are parked for inspection and good messages keep flowing instead of the partition being blocked. On the producer side I use the transactional outbox to beat the dual-write problem, writing the event into an outbox table in the same transaction as the business change so a crash can never leave a committed change without its event, with a relay publishing the outbox reliably. A circuit breaker stops the consumer from flooding a dependency that is already down, and for multi-step workflows that span services a Saga runs compensating transactions to undo steps that already committed, because a distributed database rollback is not available across services.

On my project at National Bank of India all of this came from real incidents. A consumer once credited Priya, crashed before acknowledging, and on restart the redelivered message credited her a second time, so we added an inbox-based idempotency check keyed by message id. A malformed message with a null account id failed every retry and starved the partition, so we added a dead-letter queue after three attempts. And a producer that updated the ledger then crashed before publishing left a downstream blind, so we moved to a transactional outbox. The key point I make is that these mechanisms compose: the outbox guarantees publication, at-least-once plus manual ack guarantees delivery and retry, idempotency makes redelivery safe, the DLQ contains poison, the breaker protects dependencies, and the Saga keeps the whole workflow consistent.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that a crash means the unacknowledged message is redelivered, so the real design goal is to survive redelivery safely, which I achieve with manual acknowledge-after-commit and retry, idempotent processing as the primary defense, a dead-letter queue for poison, a transactional outbox so events are never lost, a circuit breaker for failing dependencies, and a Saga with compensation for multi-step work.
